newsitem.title: GERMANY: EU official pegs 96/97 grain exports at 28 mln T.
newsitem.headline: EU official pegs 96/97 grain exports at 28 mln T.

text.p: European Union grain exports, including flour, may total 28 million tonnes in the 1996/97 season, said Roland Reifenrath, the head of grains, oilseeds and rice in the EU agriculture directorate.
Reifenrath was addressing the annual meeting of the Hamburg grain and feeds trade association.
EU grain export licences granted by April 10 totalled nearly 25 million tonnes.
The EU in 1995/96 exported 18 million tonnes of grain.
"We will be below the GATT limit on subsidised exports, but well above last year," Reifenrath said.
"The EU has shown that it has not abandoned its strategy of participating in grain exports and that it claims an important place in the third country grain market."
Reifenrath said he arrived at his estimate on the basis of a 201 million tonne crop in 1996, 170 million tonnes of domestic use and four million tonnes of imports.
Deducting the 28 million anticipated grain exports of the remaining 35 million, he arrived at a spare seven million tonnes, which he said would not automatically go into public intervention stores.
Roughly half of this amount might go into commerical stocks.
Reifenrath said the EU had to tackle prospective grain surpluses in the years to come as land set-aside, which was unpopular with farmers, was unlikely to be raised sharply.
GATT rules set strict and degressive limits on subsidised export volumes -- 32.3 million tonnes in the current season -- and import markets would not necessarily absorb all the grain on offer.
He was particularly sceptical of estimates of Chinese import needs of up to 50 million tonnes a year.
Chinese grain yields had upward potential and such a tonnage could not be handled by the current port infrastructure, he argued.

Reifenrath said it was not surprising that EU planners considered a lowering of grain intervention prices towards world market levels, especially under mounting pressure from the United States to phase out all subsidisation.
EU Commission thinking also stretched to possible future cuts of compensatory payments under 1992 farm reform stipulations.
